title: FOMC Minutes — September 15–16, 2026
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2026-09-16 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

With Kevin Warsh chairing, the Committee raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75–4.00%. The vote was a unanimous 12–0. IORB rose to 3.90% and the primary credit rate to 4.0%, both effective September 17. The standing repo rate moved to 4.0% and the reverse repo rate to 3.75%. The statement repeated that the Committee "will deliver price stability." This was an SEP meeting: eighteen participants submitted projections, which were released after the meeting.

Economic outlook

Staff expected growth to pick up in the second half of 2026 and outpace potential through 2028. Unemployment was seen staying below the staff's longer-run estimate through 2029. Staff now judged risks to employment and GDP as roughly balanced, rather than tilted to the downside as earlier in the year.

Inflation

Headline PCE was estimated at 3.8% over the 12 months to August and core at 3.4%. Under the BEA's new methodology, the estimates were 3.6% and 3.2%. Several participants pointed to core goods prices rising with the AI buildout, and some noted core services excluding housing remained elevated. Staff expected inflation to fall later this year as gasoline prices decline but now saw 2% only in 2029, with upside risks. Longer-term expectations were generally viewed as consistent with 2%. Some participants worried that more than five years above target could start to affect expectations and wage and price setting.

Labor market

Unemployment was 4.1% in July and August, and average hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the past year. Participants saw the labor market as close to maximum employment, and a majority saw modest strengthening. Several noted low hiring, low layoffs and elevated long-term unemployment.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Market pricing had moved toward a September hike, with further firming expected by year-end. Treasury yields rose about 35bp across 2- to 10-year maturities. Stocks rose modestly, led by AI-infrastructure beneficiaries, and the dollar weakened. Spreads on hyperscaler debt stayed wide compared with earlier in the year. Money markets were stable despite heavy bill issuance. The Desk paused reserve management purchases, and future purchases will be decided month by month. A late-July U.S.–Japan yen intervention used Treasury funds, not the Fed's portfolio.

Risks participants flagged

  • Persistent energy price increases from geopolitical tensions spreading into broader inflation
  • AI-related demand outpacing supply
  • Possible further tariff increases
  • Strain on lower- and moderate-income households from energy costs, plus drought and input costs hitting agriculture
  • On the other side, cybersecurity and other AI-related risks that could weigh on productivity

What it signaled about next moves

Most participants judged that another hike by year-end would likely be appropriate, while stressing they approach each meeting with an open mind. Several saw policy as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive, and a few said their estimate of the neutral rate had risen. A few urged stronger tools for handling market stress while limiting the Fed's footprint in the Treasury market.

Read-through for SPY

  • This was the first rate hike of 2026, and most participants flagged another by year-end. Higher discount rates will keep pressure on stock multiples.
  • The economic backdrop was firm: growth was expected to pick up, the labor market was near maximum employment and growth risks were balanced. That supports earnings even as rates rise.
  • AI-infrastructure names still led stocks, but wide hyperscaler credit spreads and AI-driven inflation tie that leadership to the Fed's tightening.
